extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, patent attorneys, and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and applying 35 U.S.C. § 103 obviousness rejections, including how to treat prior art, analogous art, level of ordinary skill, and the requirement to consider the claimed invention 'as a whole'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art qualifying under 35 U.S.C. 102 required to support obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a disclosure does not qualify as prior art under an appropriate section of 35 U.S.C. 102, then the disclosure is also not prior art that can be used in an obviousness rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) reference overcome by a declaration under 37 CFR 1.130(a) cannot be used in an obviousness rejection; similarly, a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) reference overcome by a declaration under 37 CFR 1.131 cannot be used in an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content of prior art must be evaluated (enablement, admissions, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The substantive content of the prior art (e.g., availability of inoperative devices, extent to which prior art must be enabling, broad disclosure rather than preferred embodiments, admissions, etc.) determines what the prior art discloses and its applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2121 - § 2129 for case law and guidance relating to how to assess the substantive content and scope of prior art disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of prior art determined at the relevant time to avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art and the obviousness inquiry must be assessed at the relevant time (pre-AIA: 'at the time the invention was made'; AIA: 'before the effective filing date of the claimed invention') to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal of hindsight-based arguments is discussed in MPEP § 2145, subsection X.A. Courts require the decisionmaker to 'cast the mind back' to the relevant time when the invention was made or before the effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) common ownership / joint research agreement requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on pre-AIA 103(c) (or to invoke its protections), the applicant has the burden of establishing that subject matter which only qualifies as prior art under subsections (e), (f) or (g) of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and used in a rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For applications pending on or after December 10, 2004, to rely on joint research provisions the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. See MPEP § 2146.02 for requirements to establish common ownership or a joint research agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement for obviousness (two-test formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is analogous art for use in an obviousness rejection if: (1) the reference is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) the reference is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two tests are separate; a reference need not meet both. If a reference is not analogous art it may not be used in an obviousness rejection. Note: there is no analogous art requirement for anticipation rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102. See In re Bigio and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must determine analogy when analyzing obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must determine whether a reference is analogous art to the claimed invention when analyzing the obviousness of the subject matter under examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When more than one prior art reference is used as the basis of an obviousness rejection, it is not required that the references be analogous art to each other. Explanations of the examiner's reasoning (e.g., why a reference is reasonably pertinent) may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining 'same field of endeavor' focuses on the reference's disclosure (embodiments, function, structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying the 'relevant field of endeavor' test, consider explanations of the invention’s subject matter in the patent application, including the embodiments, function, and structure of the claimed invention; the primary focus is on what the reference discloses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the disclosure 'in view of the reality of the circumstances' weighed from the vantage of common sense likely to be exerted by a POSITA. See Airbus and Bigio analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably pertinent test centers on the problem faced by the inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is 'reasonably pertinent' if it is relevant to the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification and 'logically [] have commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering his problem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An outside-field reference is reasonably pertinent if a person of ordinary skill would have consulted and applied its teachings when facing the inventor's problem. It may be appropriate to include an examiner's statement of understanding of the problem and factual reasons why the prior art is pertinent. The determination often turns on how the problem to be solved is perceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight similarities and differences in structure and function more than classification
rubrics_metrics.description: While Patent Office classification and cross-references provide some evidence, courts give greater weight to similarities and differences in structure and function of the inventions disclosed in the references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structural and functional overlap (e.g., related types of devices solving similar problems) rather than relying solely on class/subclass labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous-art analysis applies across technology areas (chemical, mechanical, electrical, design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous art principles are applied in different technical arts with consideration of whether practitioners would reasonably look to the cited references' fields (e.g., dye chemistry across duplicating paper art, PTFE vs rubber hose problems, rate-limiting circuits for pacemakers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factual analogies and case law examples to support analogy determinations in chemical, mechanical, electrical, and design arts (see cited cases and MPEP §1504.03 for design).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claimed invention 'as a whole' when comparing to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining differences between prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious, not whether individual differences would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim language and consider the invention and references as a whole. Avoid improperly focusing only on an isolated structural difference (see Stratoflex, Schenck examples). See MPEP § 2111 - § 2116.01 for claim interpretation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' (preserve 'as a whole' requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating the invention as if claims read differently than they do by focusing on a single advantage or feature to the exclusion of other claim limitations (see W.L. Gore and Bausch & Lomb cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of the source/cause of a problem is part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of the source of a problem can be part of the invention as a whole and may weigh against obviousness, but discovery alone does not guarantee patentability if the solution was obvious from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art contained the same solution for a similar problem, discovery of the cause may not make the subject matter patentable (see In re Sponnoble, In re Wiseman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants alleging discovery must provide substantiating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants who allege the inventor discovered the source of a problem must provide evidence substantiating that allegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable evidence includes affidavits or declarations, or a clear and persuasive assertion in the specification. Unsubstantiated statements of counsel are insufficient (see In re Wiseman, In re Kaslow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosed inherent properties are part of the 'as a whole' inquiry (but cannot rely on later-known inherency)
rubrics_metrics.description: When delineating the invention as a whole, look to properties inherent in the subject matter and disclosed in the specification; these inherent properties are considered in determining obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, obviousness cannot be predicated on what was not known at the relevant time even if inherency is later established. See In re Antonie, In re Rijckaert, and MPEP § 2112 on inherency requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must be considered in its entirety, including teachings that teach away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference must be considered as a whole, including portions that would lead away from the claimed invention; such teachings that discourage the claimed solution can affect the obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere disclosure of multiple alternatives does not necessarily teach away; teaching away requires criticism, discrediting, or discouragement of the claimed solution. See W.L. Gore and Allied Erecting examples and MPEP § 2123.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that may be considered include: (A) type of problems encountered in the art; (B) prior art solutions to those problems; (C) rapidity with which innovations are made; (D) sophistication of the technology; and (E) educational level of active workers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A POSITA is a hypothetical person presumed to know the relevant art at the relevant time and to have ordinary creativity. Examiners may consider how the specification and references reveal what is within ordinary skill. See KSR for the POSITA's creative capabilities and MPEP § 2143 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of the hypothetical person of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The person of ordinary skill is a hypothetical person of ordinary creativity (not an automaton) who is capable of fitting teachings together and making inferences and creative steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel may take into account inferences and creative steps such a person would employ. The level of disclosure in the specification can inform what is within ordinary skill (e.g., silence on how to perform a function may indicate it is within ordinary skill, provided 35 U.S.C. 112 is satisfied). See KSR and Uber Techs. v. X One examples.
